The gallery, located on OÅ¾eÅ¡kienÄs Street in central Kaunas, was launched 14 years ago by artist Vytenis Jakas. Its murals tell the story of the Jewish community that lived in the courtyard before World War Two. Scaffolding now surrounds one of the galleryâs walls as preparations begin to renovate the building. Under the current plan, the murals will be covered. âThis is a heritage site that cannot be destroyed. This would be outright vandalism,â Jakas said. Courtyard Gallery in Kaunas | Shutterstock The dispute escalated even before renovation work began. Police are investigating possible vandalism after witnesses reported seeing a resident of the building damaging the artworks with a hammer. Kaunas resident Darius PeÄiulionis said he saw a man striking the wall with a chisel and hammer. âI approached him and asked, âWhy did you do that?â He said in broken Lithuanian, âI am a resident. I donât like this. The renovation has to be done here,ââ PeÄiulionis said. Courtyard Gallery in Kaunas | LRT TV One of the damaged features was a QR code that provided information about the history depicted in the artwork in Lithuanian and English, Jakas said. The Courtyard Gallery is one of Kaunasâ most visited attractions. Tour guide Nomeda BalaseviÄiÅ«tÄ said visitors are often struck by the artwork. âThey are amazed. Everyone falls silent when they walk through here. They say they take photos, even people who donât usually take photos in this courtyard,â she said. Courtyard Gallery in Kaunas | E. BlaÅ¾ys / LRT Residents may be bothered by constant tourist flows taking snapshots, but numerous signs warn them to be quiet and respect peopleâs right to peace. By now, most of the locals have become accustomed to tourists visiting the courtyard and viewing the artworks. Jakas says he has proposed a solution that would allow the renovation to proceed while preserving the murals. He offered to repair the lower section of the wall with murals himself, at no cost to the building's residents. Courtyard Gallery in Kaunas | E. BlaÅ¾ys / LRT âI want to repair the entire lower part myself. We wouldn't take a single euro from them; they would save money,â he said. The building is located in a cultural heritage zone, and the Kaunas municipality is helping finance part of the renovation. But the artworks on the buildingâs wall were never formally authorised, and the owners did not give their consent for them to be installed. That leaves municipal officials with limited legal means to prevent their removal. Courtyard Gallery in Kaunas | E. BlaÅ¾ys / LRT âWe are all hostages of this situation. The paintings were installed without asking anyone, on the artist's initiative, so somehow we donât have the instruments to protect them,â said Saulius Rimas, head of the Kaunas municipality's Heritage Protection Division. At the same time, the municipality has acknowledged the value of the artworks. âWe have said that we see the meaning in these artworks. They are not bad,â Rimas said. BlaÅ¾ys / LRT The municipality and the buildingâs administrator have suggested alternatives that would allow both the facade to be renovated and the artworks to be preserved. But the buildingâs owners have so far rejected them. Two-thirds of the 13 owners have voted to renovate the entire wall, according to the building administrator. âIf there were other decisions, there would be other solutions. As things stand today, the solution is to repair the buildingâs facade without preserving the art installations,â said Marijus Zaborskas, head of Kaunas ButÅ³ Åªkis, the building administrator. The renovation plan could still be changed if the residents approve an alternative, Zaborskas said. https://www.delfi.lt/en/politics/no-airs.text: Delfi EN Delfi Politics 2026.09.01 18:16 No airspace incidents in Lithuania amid drone incursions in Latvia, Estonia – military Translated by Justina Vaišvilaitė-Braziulienė Source: Elta EN No airspace incidents in Lithuania amid drone incursions in Latvia, Estonia – military PHOTO: Žygimantas Gedvila | Elta Follow Delfi on Google Lithuania has not recorded any airspace breaches amid reports of drone incursions into Estonian airspace and an air alert in Latvia, the military said. "No incidents have been recorded in Lithuanian airspace, and the security situation remains unchanged. The Lithuanian Armed Forces are continuously monitoring the airspace and the regional situation and are prepared to respond, if necessary," it said in a statement to ELTA. Earlier on Tuesday, a drone crossed into southeastern Estonia, while another headed towards the eastern border town of Narva, public broadcaster ERR reported. Alerts were sent to residents, and Turkish fighter jets stationed at Estonia’s Ämari Air Base as part of NATO’s rotating air defence mission were scrambled. The threat had passed by 5:30 a.m. A late-night mobile phone alert was also issued in Latvia’s Aluksne Municipality over a potential airspace threat, LETA said. Estonia’s ERR reported that drones involved in the Latvian incident had also entered Estonian airspace, where NATO Baltic Air Policing jets continued searching for them. Lithuania’s most recent air alert was declared on 13 June in Vilnius County. Source Topics It is forbidden to copy the text of this publication without a written permission from ELTA. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Canada is the first country to have been offered associate membership of the EU. Photograph: Ronald Wittek/EPA View image in fullscreen Canada is the first country to have been offered associate membership of the EU. Photograph: Ronald Wittek/EPA Mark Carney Mark Carney calls for ‘deep cooperation’ between Canada and EU in Strasbourg speech After Trump describes associate membership as ‘laughable’, PM says majority of Canadians support closer ties with bloc Jennifer Rankin in Brussels Thu 17 Sep 2026 08.15 EDT Last modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Mark Carney has welcomed the goal of Canada becoming the EU’s first associate member, calling for “deep cooperation” between Europe and his country to secure their sovereignty, after Donald Trump derided the idea as “laughable.” In an address to the European parliament in Strasbourg, Carney said polling showed that an overwhelming majority of Canadians supported much closer ties with Europe . “Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities,” he said on Thursday, listing sectors including critical minerals, energy security and AI. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, had on Wednesday invited Canada to become the EU’s first ever associate member in a speech in which she declared she wanted to bring the bilateral relationship “to the highest level possible”. A few hours later, Trump threatened “very serious tariffs” on Europe if the plan went ahead. The EU and Canada, which already have a web of bilateral trade and sectoral agreements, have sought to move closer in recent months in the face of Trump’s trade tariffs and relentless belligerent rhetoric. Carney received a standing ovation from MEPs in Strasbourg, who waited to shake his hand and get a selfie with the Canadian leader. European lawmakers from pro-EU mainstream parties have already praised Carney’s January speech in Davos, in which he called for middle powers to work together to preserve their sovereignty in a world of great power rivalry where the strong accept no constraints. Carney reprised the theme in Strasbourg, saying: “Canada and Europe are each strong. Europe and Canada are stronger together … The objective is not self-sufficiency, it’s collective resilience.” He went on to say: “I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival, only with better manners,” saying an EU-Canada alliance would be a “beacon for other democracies”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion ‘You’re at war when you get attacked’: Mark Carney shows combative nature in face-off with Trump Read more In a speech frequently interrupted by rounds of applause, Carney detailed his plans for the future relationship, saying the two sides could cooperate on critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and computing, energy security, space and payments. He also called for “seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services”. He proposed a youth exchange programme that would enable young people to work, study and live in both jurisdictions, as well as Canadian membership of the Erasmus+ scheme, the EU’s education, training and sport programme. No country has ever been offered associate membership before, a category that does not exist in the EU’s treaties. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, floated the idea of associate membership for Ukraine as an interim step to joining the bloc earlier this year, but the idea was shot down by other member states. EU member states support the idea of closer ties with Canada, but some have reacted coolly to the name “associate membership”. Asked by a Bloomberg reporter about the concept he preferred, Carney said: “The precise nomenclature for Europe is a question for Europe,” adding that leaders and lawmakers involved “take the view [that] what matters is the substance”. He also said Canada was “not in a position, nor seeking to become, a full member of the European Union” and that the Canadian parliament would debate and vote on the future relationship. Speaking before Carney’s address, Trump warned that if the EU moved forward with the plan, Washington could impose “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe .” Responding to Trump’s overnight comments, Carney said the deepening of the EU-Canada relationship was “a positive initiative” and “not a reaction to something else”. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Anthropic co-founder and CEO, Dario Amodei, will not appear at the Greens-led Senate inquiry into AI and datacentres, but representatives are expected at a joint standing committee hearing. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters View image in fullscreen Anthropic co-founder and CEO, Dario Amodei, will not appear at the Greens-led Senate inquiry into AI and datacentres, but representatives are expected at a joint standing committee hearing. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters AI (artificial intelligence) Anthropic will not appear at Senate inquiry into AI and datacentres amid fallout from OpenAI hack Company behind Claude chatbot expected to attend separate Australian government hearing on AI next week Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Josh Taylor and Tom McIlroy Mon 28 Sep 2026 04.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 04.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The chief executive of Anthropic will turn down an invitation to appear at a Senate committee hearing on AI this week, in the wake of the revelation that OpenAI agents had breached Australian government websites. However, the company will make an appearance before another committee early next week. The chair of the Senate inquiry into AI and datacentres, Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young, wrote to OpenAI and Anthropic last week asking for their US-based chief executives to appear before the committee on Thursday this week. The invite came after the prime minister’s revelation that OpenAI’s agents had infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Neither company’s executives could be compelled to appear before the Senate committee, given they are based outside Australia, and it is understood that Anthropic – the company behind Claude – will not attend the hearing this week. It is understood the company’s local team is not in Australia, and the invite was considered last-minute. An alternative date for the hearing has been sought. It’s going to take more than an email to a public inbox to protect Australians from potential AI doom | Tom McIlroy Read more Anthropic is, however, expected to attend a separate joint standing committee hearing on AI next week. Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, will not attend, but it is understood representatives of its Australian and US operations will appear. The company has made a submission to that committee in which Anthropic warned that governments had a critical role in reinforcing a responsible approach to AI by industry, while also arguing that frontier AI was not just an economic capability but also a “national security capability”. “It matters which countries build the most capable models, and on whose terms they are deployed,” Anthropic said in the submission. “The most capable AI models are built in the United States. Broadening that development out to trusted allies like Australia is critical and will support efforts to ensure that the capability of democracies outpace those of authoritarian states.” OpenAI was approached for comment. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese , who was in the United States last week when announcing the hack, said he had spoken with OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, “to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident”. The finance and government services minister, Katy Gallagher, flagged new mandatory reporting rules could be introduced for AI data breaches. After criticism of the government’s slow response to the incident, Services Australia has put in place new procedures to ensure real-time monitoring of information sent to the public-facing email address used by OpenAI to report the hacking. ‘We can’t ignore AI or prevent it,’ Anthony Albanese tells UN general assembly – video But Gallagher rejected Coalition claims the government had politicised the Medicare breach, rejecting suggestions Labor had delayed a public announcement or overstated the significance of the rogue agent’s actions. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion “It is the first time that we’re aware that an agent acting on its own, not with the authority of OpenAI , was able to get into one of our data systems, and I think we did the right thing,” she said. Cabinet was briefed on the ongoing investigation on Monday, as the company continued to cooperate with Services Australia and the intelligence agency, the Australian Signals Directorate. Gallagher said the investigation would take a matter of weeks to be completed but confirmed the statistical website accessed in the incident had been decommissioned and the data transferred to a new portal. The taskforce would also review how OpenAI’s agent had interacted with the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare’s website. An obscure German wiki site that was reportedly hijacked and used as a message board for the agents to communicate with each other included messages showing the agents tried and failed to access the AIHW website data over multiple days in June this year, as first reported by the ABC . Part of $160m in new funding for cybersecurity improvements at Services Australia, announced in the May budget, will be used for the response to the OpenAI incident. “The kind of cyber protections of a public-facing website, versus our systems of government significance are quite different, and they are under constant, constant attention from people who would like to get in,” Gallagher said. “Those systems are the ones that the upgrade will be focused on.” The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said every cyber-attack was serious, but criticised Albanese for waiting to reveal the incident publicly. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Darya Shipilova, 28, worked at a research institute in Siberia that studies dangerous pathogens including the plague. Photograph: Social Media View image in fullscreen Darya Shipilova, 28, worked at a research institute in Siberia that studies dangerous pathogens including the plague. Photograph: Social Media Russia Plague epidemic risk in Russia low after death of lab technician, WHO says World Health Organization detects no sign of further outbreak since Darya Shipilova died last week Luke Harding and agencies Tue 6 Oct 2026 19.14 EDT First published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 08.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The World Health Organization has said the risk of an epidemic in Russia is low after the sudden death of a lab technician who worked at a plague research institute in Siberia. Darya Shipilova, who was 28, died last week, two days after falling ill. Russian media reports suggested she may have become infected after an accident at her workplace , where dangerous pathogens are kept and studied. Russian authorities have downplayed the incident and say Shipilova died of “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology” . Strict quarantine measures have been imposed at the research centre in the city of Irkutsk and in several neighbouring hospitals. Christian Lindmeier, a WHO spokesperson, said on Tuesday that there was no sign of a wider outbreak. “All ‌of the patients’ contacts have reportedly been identified and are being monitored for ‌illness, and none to date have shown ​symptoms of illness,” he said. Russian ⁠officials were still ​investigating whether viral pneumonic plague caused Shipilova’s death but the WHO had assessed the health risk as “moderate to low” for Irkutsk, “low” for the rest of Russia and “very low” for Europe , he said. WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged Russia on Tuesday to be transparent about Shipilova’s death. “Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks,” he wrote on X. 11:36 Plague outbreak? Russian lab worker dies in Siberia - The Latest According to Russian media, 60 of Shipilova’s colleagues have been locked in the institute where she worked since Friday, sleeping on the floors and chairs while tests are carried out. Similar measures have been imposed in five hospitals, with relatives forbidden to see patients. The Kremlin’s spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, urged people on Tuesday not to listen to rumours but to rely on statements from Russia’s health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor. It said the situation in Irkutsk was stable , with no new infectious disease cases reported among institute employees. Washington has been watching developments closely . The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, called on Moscow on Tuesday to release more details about the case. “I think it’s incumbent upon ⁠Russia to obviously share more information with ​the world,” he said. “We’re watching it very closely, hour ‌by hour.” The Wall Street Journal reported that the US state department had sent Russia a confidential diplomatic communication known as a demarche warning Moscow that failure to disclose details runs counter to its international health obligations. Trump said on Tuesday that he was due to speak shortly with Russian president Vladimir Putin about the technician’s death. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion “I have a call scheduled, yes,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he had spoken to Putin on the issue yet, adding that it would happen “very soon”. Trump had said earlier that his administration was willing to offer assistance. “I hate to see them having it. We’ll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we’ll always help,” he told reporters. In an apparent mirror response, Rospotrebnadzor announced that Russia was prepared to assist the US in combating its own outbreaks of infectious diseases. “The situation regarding dangerous infectious diseases remains unstable,” it said, highlighting a “significantly worsened” measles situation in three US states and a “fatal case of plague” recorded in New Mexico in June. *With Agence France-Presse Explore more on these topics Russia Europe Bubonic plague World Health Organization Health news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
